claims.reason: S1 directly defines checkpointing as transferring WAL transactions into the database.
S3 specifies the post-commit trigger at N or more frames. The claim does not explicitly establish connection-local configuration.
S3 explicitly identifies automatic checkpoints as PASSIVE.
S1 establishes the active-reader end mark as the boundary that stops checkpoint progress.
S1 requires WAL synchronization before transferring content. This states only one part of the rubric's complete synchronization order.
S1 requires database synchronization before WAL reset. This complements f5 rather than duplicating it.
S2 specifies maximum available progress without waiting. The claim omits the explicit busy-handler and incomplete-checkpoint provisions.
S1 directly connects increasing WAL size to proportional lookup cost and degraded reads. The rubric's checkpoint-scheduling implication is not stated.
S1 explains the precise overwrite hazard beyond a reader's end mark. This adds the causal explanation for f4.
S1 describes saved checkpoint progress in the wal-index and resumption at the next invocation.
S2 specifies FULL's writer and reader waiting conditions and busy-handler use. The claim omits continued admission of new readers.
S2 explicitly states that pending FULL checkpoints block new writers.
S2 gives both the additional database-only reader condition and its consequence for the next writer.
S2 specifies RESTART behavior plus truncation to zero bytes immediately before successful return.
S2 defines NOOP as checkpointing zero frames while exposing the two status outputs.
S2 specifies SQLITE_BUSY on checkpoint-lock contention. The busy-handler exception is not included in this claim.
S1 assigns the default checkpoint to the threshold-crossing COMMIT thread. The claim does not state the resulting commit-latency consequence.
S1 supplies the exact version, release date, and qualified proportional-size statement.
S2 specifies the refusal conditions and PASSIVE fallback. The claim omits the resulting SQLITE_BUSY return.
S2 describes writer-lock retry behavior and both termination conditions when a busy-handler is configured.
S2 explicitly excludes busy-handler invocation for checkpoint-lock contention. This adds a distinct fact to f16 but does not itself state SQLITE_BUSY.
S2 explicitly includes previously checkpointed frames in pnCkpt. The broader counter and sentinel semantics are absent.
S3 states that zero or negative N disables automatic checkpoints.
S3 states that installing autocheckpoint replaces an existing WAL-hook callback. This gives only one direction of the rubric's reciprocal replacement.
S3 states that installing a WAL hook disables configured autocheckpointing. This is the reverse interaction, not a duplicate of f24.
S1 explicitly links continuously overlapping readers to checkpoint starvation and unbounded WAL growth.
S1 identifies reader-free intervals combined with checkpoint attempts as the remedy for reader starvation.
S1 explicitly prohibits WAL reset during an ongoing write transaction.
S2 permits new readers during pending FULL checkpoints. This complements the waiting and writer-exclusion claims without repeating them.
S1 states the combined transfer, synchronization, and reader conditions for writer-driven WAL rewind.
S1 directly supports normal non-truncation and the named exception. The claim does not explicitly state recycling.
S1 explicitly assigns sync operations exclusively to checkpointing under synchronous=NORMAL in the WAL context.
S1 states that NORMAL omits commit-time WAL synchronization. The power-loss rollback consequence is absent.
S2 specifies NULL or empty selection of all attached WAL databases and undefined counters in that case. Error-dependent abandonment is absent.
S2 explicitly describes continued processing and eventual SQLITE_BUSY for busy errors in the multi-database operation. Other-error abandonment is not stated.
S2 gives SQLITE_OK and both -1 outputs for a named attached database outside WAL mode. This does not cover the rubric's complete counter semantics.

Claims establish threshold triggering, disabling, and callback interactions.
Claims establish end-mark boundaries, saved progress, starvation, and reader-gap mitigation.
Claims establish persistence ordering and checkpoint synchronization under NORMAL.
Claims establish nonwaiting checkpoint progress and automatic use of this mode.
Claims establish specific waiting conditions, writer exclusion, and continued reader admission.
f13 establishes the additional reader condition that enables the next writer to restart the WAL.
f14 establishes physical truncation on successful return, distinct from RESTART.
f15 establishes status retrieval without checkpointing frames.
Claims establish distinct lock-contention paths, retry conditions, and fallback behavior.
Claims connect WAL size to read cost and identify the thread that executes automatic checkpoints.
Claims establish reset preconditions and normal non-truncation; these are distinct from merely transferring frames.

concepts.canonical_name: WAL reader page lookup and shared-memory index
concepts.reason: f8 supports the distinct lookup-cost idea, although detailed lookup and shared-memory architecture remain undeveloped. General reader lookup is adjacent to internal checkpointing.

overall_limitations: All 36 claims are source-supported; no pair repeats the same fact with the same specifics.
Several composite rubric entries are distributed across separate claims. Individual gold_ids require adequate coverage of the whole entry; an empty list does not indicate a false claim.
Coverage omits reader end-mark fixation, shared-memory host restrictions, the one-writer limit, the default 1000-page threshold, and several API failure and durability consequences.
The reported pass counts and information rates do not establish claim depth or research saturation.
